description: Practice sets for the grammar topics that had none, written by hand (2026-10-13). Imported and published.

lessons.title: Some or Any? Countable and Uncountable Nouns
lessons.description: Practise countable and uncountable nouns with some, any, a and an.

exercises.prompt: There is ___ milk in the fridge.
exercises.explanation: Milk is uncountable, and in a positive sentence we use some.

exercises.prompt: Have we got ___ bread for sandwiches?
exercises.explanation: Bread is uncountable, and in questions we usually use any.

exercises.prompt: I'd like ___ apple, please.
exercises.explanation: Apple is countable and singular, and it starts with a vowel sound, so we say an apple.

exercises.prompt: We haven't got ___ eggs. Let's buy some. (some / any)
exercises.explanation: In negative sentences we use any.

exercises.prompt: Can I have ___ water, please? (some / any)
exercises.explanation: When we ask for something politely, we use some even in a question.

exercises.prompt: “I need an advice” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Advice is uncountable: we say some advice or a piece of advice.

exercises.prompt: “There are some bananas on the table” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Bananas is a plural countable noun, so are some is correct.

exercises.prompt: There ___ some cheese on the pizza.
exercises.explanation: Cheese is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: is.

exercises.prompt: Match each noun with the correct phrase.
exercises.explanation: Uncountable nouns (music, information) take some; singular countable nouns take a or an.
In questions with there are we use any: Are there any cookies left?

exercises.prompt: There isn't ___ rice in the cupboard. (some / any)
exercises.explanation: Negative sentence, so we use any.

exercises.prompt: She has ___ good news for us!
exercises.explanation: News is uncountable, even though it ends in -s, so we say some news.

lessons.title: Much, Many, A Lot Of
lessons.description: Practise much, many and a lot of with countable and uncountable nouns.

exercises.prompt: How ___ friends do you have on this app?
exercises.explanation: Friends is countable, so we ask How many.

exercises.prompt: How ___ time do we have before the film starts?
exercises.explanation: Time is uncountable, so we ask How much.

exercises.prompt: I don't drink ___ coffee.
exercises.explanation: Coffee is uncountable; in negatives we use much.

exercises.prompt: There aren't ___ people at the party yet. (much / many)
exercises.explanation: People is countable plural, so we use many.

exercises.prompt: She has got a ___ of games on her phone.
exercises.explanation: A lot of works with countable and uncountable nouns in positive sentences.

exercises.prompt: “How much books have you got?” is a correct question.
exercises.explanation: Books is countable, so we say How many books.

exercises.prompt: “We haven't got much money” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Money is uncountable, so much is correct in a negative sentence.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginning with the right ending.

pairs.How much sugar: do you want in your tea?

exercises.explanation: many + countable plural; much + uncountable; a lot of + both in positive sentences.
How many + plural noun + are: How many songs are on your playlist?

exercises.prompt: I've got ___ homework tonight. I can't go out.
exercises.explanation: Homework is uncountable; in a positive sentence we use a lot of.

exercises.prompt: There isn't ___ milk left. (much / many)
exercises.explanation: Milk is uncountable, so much.

lessons.title: The Best, the Biggest: Superlatives
lessons.description: Practise superlative adjectives: the tallest, the most interesting, the best.

exercises.prompt: Mount Everest is ___ mountain in the world.
exercises.explanation: Short adjective + -est, with the: the highest.

exercises.prompt: This is ___ game I have ever played!
exercises.explanation: Good is irregular: good – better – the best.

exercises.prompt: Maths is the ___ subject for me. (difficult)
exercises.explanation: Long adjectives use the most: the most difficult.

exercises.prompt: Today is the ___ day of the year. (hot)
exercises.explanation: Hot has one vowel + one consonant, so we double the t: hottest.

exercises.prompt: That was the ___ film ever. It was so boring! (bad)
exercises.explanation: Bad is irregular: bad – worse – the worst.

exercises.prompt: “She is the most tall girl in our class” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Tall is short, so we say the tallest, not the most tall.

exercises.prompt: “This is the most beautiful beach in Spain” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: Beautiful is long, so the most beautiful is correct.

exercises.prompt: My little brother is ___ person in our family.
exercises.explanation: Adjectives ending in -y change to -iest: funny – the funniest.

exercises.prompt: Match the adjective with its superlative.
exercises.explanation: Short: -est (double the last letter after a short vowel); -y: -iest; long: the most; far is irregular.
the most + long adjective + noun.

exercises.prompt: Who is the ___ singer in the world right now? (famous)
exercises.explanation: Famous has two syllables and doesn't end in -y, so the most famous.

exercises.prompt: This is ___ coffee in town.
exercises.explanation: Cheap is a short adjective: the cheapest.

lessons.title: Always, Often, Never: Adverbs of Frequency
lessons.description: Practise always, usually, often, sometimes and never and where to put them.

exercises.prompt: I ___ check my phone in the morning. Every single day!
exercises.explanation: Every single day = always (100%).

exercises.prompt: She ___ eats meat. She is a vegetarian.
exercises.explanation: A vegetarian doesn't eat meat at all, so never (0%).
The adverb goes before the main verb: We usually play.
With the verb be, the adverb goes after it: is often late.

exercises.prompt: “I go always to the gym” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: The adverb goes before the main verb: I always go to the gym.

exercises.prompt: “They are never at home on Sundays” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: With be, the adverb comes after it: are never.

exercises.prompt: Match the adverb with how often it means.
exercises.explanation: always > usually > sometimes > never.

exercises.prompt: How often do you ___ to music?
exercises.explanation: After do you we use the base form: listen.

exercises.prompt: My cat ___ sleeps on my bed, but not every night. (sometimes / never)
exercises.explanation: Not every night but sometimes: about 50%.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I am usually tired after school.
I usually am tired after school.
Usually I tired am after school.
exercises.answer: I am usually tired after school.
exercises.explanation: With be, the adverb goes after the verb: am usually.

exercises.prompt: Tom is a great student. He ___ forgets his homework. (always / never)
exercises.explanation: A great student doesn't forget homework: never.

lessons.title: Future with Will
lessons.description: Practise will for predictions, promises and quick decisions, and won't for the negative.

exercises.prompt: Don't worry, I ___ help you with your homework.
exercises.explanation: A promise about the future: I will help you.

exercises.prompt: It's cold. I think it ___ snow tonight.
exercises.explanation: A prediction with I think: it will snow.

exercises.prompt: I'm sorry, I ___ be late again. I promise! (negative)
exercises.explanation: The negative of will is will not / won't.

exercises.prompt: “She will goes to the party” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: After will we use the base form: She will go.

exercises.prompt: “Will you come to my birthday?” is a correct question.
exercises.explanation: Questions: Will + subject + base verb.
Subject + will + base verb.
Question: Will + subject + verb.

exercises.prompt: “The phone is ringing.” “I ___ answer it!”
exercises.explanation: A quick decision at the moment of speaking: I'll answer it.

exercises.prompt: Match the situation with the use of will.
exercises.explanation: will is used for predictions, promises and decisions made right now.

exercises.prompt: Maybe they ___ win the match. (will / are)
exercises.explanation: Maybe + will for a prediction we are not sure about.

exercises.prompt: I'm hungry. I think I ___ make a sandwich.
exercises.explanation: A decision right now: I'll make a sandwich.

lessons.title: Must or Have To?
lessons.description: Practise must, have to, mustn't and don't have to for rules and obligations.

exercises.prompt: You ___ wear a seatbelt in the car. It's the law.
exercises.explanation: A rule from outside (the law): you have to.

exercises.prompt: She ___ get up early tomorrow. Her train is at 6.
exercises.explanation: With she we use has to.

exercises.prompt: You ___ use your phone during the exam. It's not allowed!
exercises.explanation: mustn't = it is not allowed.

exercises.prompt: It's Saturday! We ___ go to school today.
exercises.explanation: don't have to = it isn't necessary (but it's allowed).

exercises.prompt: “You mustn't pay. It's free” means it is not allowed to pay.
exercises.explanation: For something free we say you don't have to pay — it isn't necessary.

exercises.prompt: “He musts go home now” is a correct sentence.
exercises.explanation: must never changes: He must go home now.

exercises.prompt: Does he ___ to wear a uniform at his school? (have / has)
exercises.explanation: After does we use the base form: Does he have to…?

exercises.prompt: Match the sentence with its meaning.
exercises.explanation: mustn't = not allowed; don't have to = not necessary; must = necessary.
Subject + have to + base verb.

exercises.prompt: You ___ shout in the library. It's a quiet place. (mustn't / don't have to)
exercises.explanation: Shouting is not allowed in the library: mustn't.

exercises.prompt: I ___ to walk the dog every evening.
exercises.explanation: have to: I have to walk the dog. (must is never followed by to.)
